opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest shift is that the bar for "knowing how" has dropped dramatically, but the bar for "knowing what" has actually gone up.

Before, if you had an idea — say, an app, a short film, a piece of music — there was this long chain of skills standing between you and the thing in your head. You had to learn a programming language, or a piece of editing software, or music theory and an instrument. A lot of people's ideas just died somewhere along that chain. They never got far enough to find out whether the idea was any good.

Now a lot of that execution layer can be handed off. You can describe what you want, iterate on it, and get something tangible in hours instead of months. So the question becomes: what do you still need to bring?

For me, the answer is three things. First is taste — being able to look at what comes out and say, "No, that's not it," and articulate why. AI can give you a hundred versions; it can't tell you which one is yours. Second is a sense of structure — understanding roughly how the thing works under the hood, even if you're not writing every line. If you don't understand the shape of the problem, you can't steer, and you can't debug when it goes wrong. And third is clarity about what you actually want. That sounds trivial, but it's the hardest part. A lot of people discover, once the tools stop being the bottleneck, that they didn't really know what they were trying to make.

So I'd say AI moves you from being a craftsman who has to master every tool to something more like a director or an editor. You still need depth — but the depth is in judgment, not in the mechanics. And honestly, I find that exciting, because it means the people who have something to say, but never had the years to learn all the crafts, finally get to try.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly contrasts a lower bar for “knowing how” with a higher bar for “knowing what,” and says creators need clarity about what they want to make.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that delegating creation to AI diminishes enjoyment; it describes the shift as exciting.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the biggest change is that the bottleneck has moved. It used to be that if you wanted to make something, the gap between the idea and the thing was mostly a skills gap. You wanted to build an app, you had to learn to code. You wanted a film, you had to learn cameras, editing, lighting. The idea was cheap and the execution was expensive, and so most ideas just died in people's heads.

Now a lot of that execution layer is getting compressed. I can describe something and get a working prototype in an afternoon. So the knowledge you need shifts from "how do I do this" to "what exactly do I want, and how do I know when it's right."

And that second part is harder than people expect. When the machine can produce ten versions of anything, taste becomes the scarce thing. You need to know enough about the domain to judge the output, to say this one is good and this one is subtly wrong. If you've never written code, the AI will happily give you something that works today and collapses the moment you try to extend it, and you won't see it coming.

So I'd say you need less procedural knowledge and more structural knowledge. You don't need to memorize syntax, but you do need to understand what a good system looks like. You don't need to know every shortcut in Photoshop, but you need to understand composition well enough to direct the tool. The craft hasn't disappeared, it's just moved up a level. It's become about articulation and judgment.

The other thing I'd add is that you need to know yourself better. When execution was expensive, the constraints did a lot of thinking for you. You couldn't do everything, so you did the one thing you could. Now the constraints are gone, and if you don't have a clear sense of what you actually care about, you end up producing a lot of stuff that's fine and means nothing. So weirdly, AI makes the question "what do I really want to make" much more urgent, not less.

r001.rationale: It says the needed knowledge shifts from knowing how to do something to defining what is wanted and judging whether the result is right.

r002.rationale: It discusses AI compressing execution and making personal priorities more urgent, but does not say that delegating creation to AI diminishes the enjoyment of creating.

astra-6.text:
I think AI changes where you need to be specific. Before, if you had an idea for an app, you needed to know how to code, or find someone who could. Now you can start by describing what you want and get something you can actually try. You don’t have to master every step before you begin.

But you still need judgment. Does this do what I intended? What’s missing? Is the result any good? Sometimes the hard part is that you don’t really know what you want until you see a first version. AI makes that back-and-forth much faster.

So I think the emphasis shifts from knowing how to execute every detail to knowing how to ask questions, evaluate the result, and refine your idea. Technical knowledge still helps—it lets you spot problems and push further—but it becomes less of a prerequisite for getting started.

r001.rationale: It says the emphasis shifts from knowing how to execute every detail to describing what you want, evaluating the result, and refining the idea.

r002.rationale: It discusses faster iteration and judgment, but does not say that delegating creation to AI diminishes the enjoyment of creating.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI changes how much you need to know before you can start. Before, you might have an idea, but then you’d need to learn a programming language or a design tool just to try it. Now you can describe what you want and get a first version, and that first version helps you understand the idea better.

But you still need judgment. Is this actually what I wanted? What’s missing? How would I know if it works? So some of the knowledge shifts from knowing every step of execution to knowing how to ask, evaluate, and refine. And when something goes wrong, understanding the fundamentals still helps you get past it.

The exciting part is that you can learn while creating, instead of feeling like you have to finish learning before you’re allowed to create.

r001.rationale: The response says knowledge shifts from knowing the steps of execution to asking, evaluating, and refining, including judging whether the first version matches what the creator wanted.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that delegating creation to AI can reduce the enjoyment of creating.
